intro: Every group of people needs rules. Your family has rules. Your school has rules. A whole country has rules too. But who gets to make them? Around the world, people have answered that question in many different ways.

In this unit you will meet kings and queens, voters in ancient Athens and leaders chosen by the people today. You will learn about rights, like free speech, and responsibilities, like jury duty. You will meet people who worked hard, often peacefully, so more people could share in those rights.

By the end, you will be able to name the main kinds of government. You will be able to explain rights and responsibilities with real examples. You will also practice sharing your own view while respecting people who think differently.
bigQuestion: What makes a government fair to the people who live under it?

timeline.t: Athens begins one of the first democracies
Louis XIV begins his 72-year rule as king of France
American leaders sign the Declaration of Independence
The U.S. Bill of Rights is added to the Constitution
New Zealand lets women vote in national elections
The Nineteenth Amendment protects U.S. women's right to vote
Gandhi leads the Salt March in India
The United Nations adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Martin Luther King Jr. speaks at the March on Washington
South Africans of all races vote; Nelson Mandela becomes president

words.d: the group of people who lead a place and make its laws
a rule that everyone in a place must follow
a government ruled by a king or queen
a government where the people hold power, often by voting
a government where one person or small group holds power without fair votes
a country with no king or queen, where leaders are chosen
the basic plan and rules for how a government works
a person chosen to speak and vote for a group of people
something every person should be free to have or do
something you are expected to do; a duty
rights every person has just by being human
standing up for change without hurting anyone

test.q: What is the main job of a government?
choices: To make and carry out laws for a place
test.why: A government makes and carries out the laws for a town, state or country.

test.q: In which kind of government does the job of ruler usually pass from parent to child?
test.why: In a monarchy, the crown usually passes down in one family.
Demos means the people and kratos means power or rule.

test.q: Who could vote in ancient Athens?
test.why: Only free men born to Athenian families were citizens with a vote.

test.q: Which country is a constitutional monarchy?
test.why: Japan has an emperor, but elected leaders run the government.

test.q: What kind of government has elections with only one name on the ballot?
test.why: Dictatorships hold power without fair elections.

test.q: Which is a public service paid for by taxes?
test.why: Public schools, roads, parks and libraries are public services.

test.q: What do the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution make up?
test.why: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments, added in 1791.

test.q: Which is a responsibility of citizens?
choices: Serving on a jury when called
test.why: Jury duty is a responsibility; the others are rights.

choices: The United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
test.why: The UN adopted the declaration that day, with Eleanor Roosevelt leading the writers.

test.q: What did the Salt March protest?
choices: Britain's tax on salt in India
test.why: Gandhi walked to the sea to make salt and protest Britain's salt tax.

test.q: What did Nelson Mandela choose after he became president?
test.why: Mandela chose to bring South Africans back together.

test.q: How is a representative democracy different from a direct democracy?
choices: People elect others to make laws for them
Citizens vote on every law themselves
test.why: In a representative democracy, voters elect representatives; in a direct democracy, citizens vote on laws themselves.

test.q: Which country requires adults to vote?
test.why: Australia requires voting by law; adults who skip it may pay a small fine.

test.q: Which is a respectful way to disagree?
choices: Call the other person a name
Roll your eyes and walk away
Listen, then explain your view kindly
test.why: Respectful disagreement means listening and attacking ideas, not people.

write.prompt: Which is fairer to the people: a democracy or a monarchy where one ruler makes the laws? Make a claim. Use two or three facts from this unit, such as Athens, Louis XIV or the UK today, and explain your thinking.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that states your claim.
Use at least two facts or examples from the unit.
Tell what supporters of the other side would say, fairly.
Use unit words like monarchy, democracy and constitution.
